lessons.title: Temperature, thermometers and expansion
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Thermal physics: temperature, expansion, gas laws, heat capacity, change of state, heat transfer (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)

objectives: Distinguish heat and temperature and describe the kinetic model of matter.
Describe liquid-in-glass thermometers, fixed points and the Kelvin scale.
Describe expansion of solids, liquids and gases and its uses and problems.
Use T(K) = θ(°C) + 273 and the linear scale of a thermometer.
reviewNotes: Kelvin conversion uses 273 (273.15 is more exact). Anomalous expansion of water (4 °C) may be in the syllabus; not detailed here.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Heat and temperature
blocks.md: **Heat** is energy transferred because of a temperature difference (joule). **Temperature** measures how hot something is (°C or K): it is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles. In solids particles vibrate in fixed places, in liquids they slide past each other, in gases they move freely and far apart.

blocks.title: Thermometers and scales
blocks.md: A liquid-in-glass thermometer uses the expansion of mercury or coloured alcohol. Fixed points: **0 °C** (pure melting ice) and **100 °C** (steam above boiling water at normal pressure); the scale in between is divided into 100 equal steps. **Kelvin scale**: $T(K) = \theta(°C) + 273$; 0 K (−273 °C) is the lowest possible temperature.

blocks.title: Expansion
blocks.md:
When heated, most solids, liquids and gases **expand** (particles vibrate or move more). Gases expand most, solids least.

- Uses: **bimetallic strip** (two metals bend as they heat unequally) in thermostats and fire alarms.
- Problems: gaps are left in railway lines and bridges; telephone and power cables sag in hot weather.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Heat and temperature are not the same: a bath of lukewarm water holds more heat than a hot cup of tea.
- A temperature **difference** has the same number in °C and K, but a temperature itself does not.

blocks.caption: A thermometer with fixed points at 0 °C and 100 °C; the column length changes linearly with temperature.
blocks.alt: A vertical liquid thermometer with marks at 0 and 100 degrees Celsius and a marked level at 35 degrees Celsius.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Kelvin
blocks.statement: The temperature in Buea one morning is 27 °C. Express it in kelvin, and give 400 K in °C.

blocks.title: Example 2 — uncalibrated thermometer
blocks.statement: The mercury thread of an unmarked thermometer is 2 cm long at 0 °C and 22 cm long at 100 °C. Find the temperature when the thread is 9 cm long.
steps: Length change for 100 °C = 22 − 2 = 20 cm, so 0.2 cm per °C.
Change from the ice point = 9 − 2 = 7 cm, so θ = 7 ÷ 0.2 = 35 °C.

reviewNotes: Whether the Board expects the combined formula P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ should be confirmed (it follows from the three laws).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Gas pressure
blocks.md: Gas particles move randomly and hit the walls of their container. The impacts of many particles give a steady **pressure**. Heating the gas makes the particles faster, so the pressure (or volume) increases; compressing a gas into a smaller volume means more collisions with the walls.

blocks.title: The three gas laws (fixed mass of gas)
blocks.md:
- **Boyle's law** (constant T): $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$ — pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
- **Charles's law** (constant P): $\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$.
- **Pressure law** (constant V): $\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$.

**T must be in kelvin.** The same units may be used for P (or V) on both sides.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Never use °C in Charles's or the pressure law: add 273 first.
- Boyle's law needs the **temperature to stay constant**; a fast pump heats the air.
- A graph of P against V at constant T is a **curve**; P against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.

blocks.caption: Boyle's law: pressure falls as volume rises, PV is constant (here PV = 60 in arbitrary units).
blocks.alt: A downward curve of pressure against volume with two marked points where the product of pressure and volume is 60.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Boyle's law
blocks.statement: Air of volume 600 cm³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is compressed slowly to 200 cm³ at constant temperature. Find the new pressure.

blocks.title: Example 2 — car tyre
blocks.statement: A tyre (volume taken as constant) has air at 2.4 × 10⁵ Pa at 27 °C. After a long drive the air is at 57 °C. Find the new pressure.
steps: Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 330 K.

lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Thermal physics: temperature, expansion, gas laws, heat capacity, change of state, heat transfer (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity.
Use Q = mcΔθ and Pt = mcΔθ for electric heating.
Use the method of mixtures (heat lost = heat gained).
Explain why water is used as a coolant and for heating.
reviewNotes: Values used: c(water) = 4200 J/kg °C; c(copper) about 400, c(aluminium) about 900, c(iron) about 450 J/kg °C — rounded school values; check against the school table.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Specific heat capacity
blocks.md: The **specific heat capacity (c)** of a substance is the energy needed to raise the temperature of **1 kg** by **1 °C** (unit **J/kg °C**). Water: c = **4200 J/kg °C** (this value is used in this course). The **heat capacity** of an object = mass × c (J/°C).

blocks.caption: Q in joules, m in kg, Δθ = change in temperature (°C)

blocks.title: Electric heater and mixtures
blocks.md:
- For an electric heater of power P working for time t (no losses): $Pt = mc\Delta\theta$.
- **Method of mixtures**: when a hot and a cold liquid are mixed, **heat lost by the hot = heat gained by the cold** (if no heat is lost to the surroundings).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Mass must be in **kg** (500 g = 0.5 kg).
- Δθ = final − initial temperature.
- Real experiments lose heat to the air and the container, so measured c is usually a bit too high.

blocks.caption: Approximate specific heat capacities: water needs much more energy per kg per degree than metals.
blocks.alt: A bar chart: copper about 400, iron about 450, aluminium about 900 and water 4200 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

blocks.title: Example 1 — heating water
blocks.statement: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water from 25 °C to 75 °C? How long does a 2 kW heater take (no losses)?

blocks.title: Example 2 — mixing water
blocks.statement: 0.5 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 1.5 kg of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature (ignore losses).
steps: Let the final temperature be θ. Heat lost = 0.5 × 4200 × (80 − θ); heat gained = 1.5 × 4200 × (θ − 20).

objectives: Describe melting, boiling, evaporation, condensation and freezing using particles.
Explain why temperature stays constant during a change of state.
Define specific latent heat and use Q = ml.
Distinguish evaporation from boiling.
reviewNotes: Values used: specific latent heat of fusion of ice 336 000 J/kg; of vaporisation of water 2 260 000 J/kg (2.26 × 10⁶). Some school tables use 340 000 and 2 300 000.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Latent heat
blocks.md: While a substance melts or boils, it takes in energy but the **temperature stays constant**: the energy breaks the forces between particles instead of speeding them up. The **specific latent heat** is the energy needed to change **1 kg** of a substance from one state to another **without a change of temperature**: $Q = ml$ (J/kg).

blocks.title: Values for water (used here)
blocks.md:
- Specific latent heat of **fusion** (ice → water at 0 °C): **336 000 J/kg**.
- Specific latent heat of **vaporisation** (water → steam at 100 °C): **2 260 000 J/kg**.

Vaporisation needs much more energy because the particles must be pulled completely apart.

blocks.title: Evaporation and boiling
blocks.md: **Boiling** happens throughout the liquid at one fixed temperature (the boiling point). **Evaporation** happens only at the surface, at any temperature, and it **cools** the liquid because the fastest particles escape. It is faster when warm, windy, with a large surface and dry air (that is why washing dries well in the dry season).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Use Q = mcΔθ when the temperature **changes**; use Q = ml when the **state** changes at constant temperature.
- On a heating curve the flat parts are the changes of state.

blocks.caption: Heating curve of ice to steam: flat parts are melting at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C.
blocks.alt: A temperature-time graph: a rise from −10 to 0 °C, a flat part at 0 °C, a rise to 100 °C, and a flat part at 100 °C.

blocks.title: Example 1 — melting ice
blocks.statement: How much energy melts 0.2 kg of ice already at 0 °C?

blocks.title: Example 2 — ice to warm water
blocks.statement: Find the energy to change 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C.
steps: Warming the water from 0 °C to 20 °C: Q₂ = 0.5 × 4200 × 20 = 42 000 J.

lessons.title: Conduction, convection and radiation
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Thermal physics: temperature, expansion, gas laws, heat capacity, change of state, heat transfer (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe how conduction, convection and radiation transfer heat.
Explain which surfaces are good absorbers and emitters.
Explain the construction of a vacuum flask.
Apply the ideas to everyday situations such as cooking, houses and clothes.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Three ways heat travels
blocks.md:
- **Conduction**: transfer through a material by vibrating particles passing on energy (best in metals, which also have free electrons). Needs matter; main way in solids.
- **Convection**: in liquids and gases, warm fluid becomes less dense and rises, cool fluid sinks, setting up a current.
- **Radiation**: infrared waves; needs no medium; travels through a vacuum (heat from the Sun).

blocks.title: Surfaces
blocks.md: Dull **black** surfaces are the best **absorbers and emitters** of radiation; shiny, light-coloured surfaces are the best **reflectors** and the worst emitters. Hence houses in hot regions are painted white, and cooking pots are black on the bottom but shiny on the outside to cut heat loss.

blocks.title: Vacuum flask
blocks.md: The flask has two glass walls with a **vacuum** between (no conduction or convection), **silvered** surfaces (reflect radiation) and a **stopper** that is a poor conductor (cuts conduction and convection at the top). Hot drinks stay hot and cold drinks stay cold.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Convection and conduction are different: convection needs a fluid that can move.
- Metals feel colder than wood at the same temperature because they conduct heat away from your hand faster, not because they are colder.

blocks.caption: A vacuum flask: double wall with a vacuum between silvered surfaces.
blocks.alt: A flask drawn as two nested containers with a gap labelled vacuum, a hot liquid inside and a stopper on top.

blocks.title: Example 1 — metal and wood
blocks.statement: Explain why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon when both have been in the same room.
steps: Both are at room temperature, which is lower than your hand.
Metal is a good conductor, so it removes heat from your hand quickly and feels cold; wood is a poor conductor, so little heat leaves your hand.
blocks.answer: Metal conducts heat away from the hand faster.

blocks.title: Example 2 — heating water in a kettle
blocks.statement: Explain how the whole of the water in a kettle is heated when the element is at the bottom.
steps: Water near the element warms, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises.
Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place; the circulating convection current heats all the water.
